consensus_summary: A sign is a perceptible event, act, object, or token that points beyond itself to divine activity, revelation, promise, or authority. Miraculous authentication is prominent, but covenant tokens, prophetic sign-acts, and eschatological indicators are also recognized.
book_summary: A sign is a marked witness to God's word, specifically either an anticipatory prophetic word, scene, or lived similitude whose fulfillment testifies, or an enduring covenant token witnessing to an established word. It need not be a demanded miracle.
consensus_core_identification: A divinely significant pointer or witness that communicates or authenticates divine reality, revelation, promise, or authority.
book_core_identification: A marked witness by which God makes his word known, through fulfilled prophetic representation or a continuing covenant token.
boundary_disagreement: The book restricts signs to two word-witnessing classes: anticipatory prophetic signs confirmed by fulfillment and continuing covenant tokens. The broader consensus also admits miracles authenticating messengers, cosmic or eschatological portents, and other revelatory indicators without requiring that they fit either class. The book also resists treating miraculous character or performance on demand as definitional.
material_contradiction: There is no contradiction in the shared identification of signs as pointers or witnesses to divine revelation. The material disagreement concerns whether the broader class of authenticating miracles and other divine indicators counts as signs apart from prophetic fulfillment or covenant-token functions.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus's central functional category—a perceptible witness pointing beyond itself to God's revelation—but gives it a more restrictive extension and organization. Covenant signs and prophetic sign-acts are expressly present among the consensus alternatives, so the identification is neither novel nor a replacement of the consensus core. It is refined because the book elevates those cases into an apparently exhaustive two-part definition and declines to define signs primarily by miraculous authentication.
strongest_objection: The apparent narrowing may be overstated: the consensus already says that a sign is not merely a wonder and explicitly includes covenant tokens and prophetic sign-acts. Moreover, the book does not categorically exclude miracles; many miraculous signs could qualify as prophetic scenes whose fulfillment or occurrence witnesses to God's word. The printed texts strongly illustrate the book's selected cases, but they do not by themselves establish that all biblical signs must belong exclusively to its two classes.
